```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Anchor here() to this post so paths work no matter where R starts
here::i_am("posts/welcome/index.qmd")

# House colours, ggplot2 theme, and the packages every post uses
source(here::here("R", "theme_cwr.R"))

# Data download bundle helpers; data_bundle_version is the release version linked at the end.
# Bump it when the data changes and /publish rebuilds the bundle.
source(here::here("R", "data_bundle.R"))
data_bundle_version <- 1

# Post-specific packages go here, and in R/packages.R
library(sf)        # spatial data held as a data frame with a geometry column
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data

# Small tidy files produced by R/02_clean_data.R live in data/
districts <- read_sf(here("posts", "welcome", "data", "districts.geojson"))

# How people live: the share of households that are a couple with children at
# home, the average number of people in a household, and the share of dwellings
# that are single-detached houses. 2021 census.
households <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "households.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Mother tongue and the language spoken at home, 2021 census.
# Cattle and people in each of the four townships on 11 May 2021, from the
# Census of Agriculture and the census population count. Four rows.
cattle <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "cattle.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

language <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "language.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Median household and median individual income from the 2021 census, which
# reports income earned in 2020, restated in 2026 dollars by 02_clean_data.R.
# Eight rows: the seven municipalities and the Region as a whole.
income <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "income.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

Waterloo Region, formally known as the Regional Municipality of Waterloo, comprises three cities and four townships. In this introductory post, we'll take a look at a few charts that highlight key differences between the Region's urban and rural constituents, differences that will be explored in more detail in future posts. Readers familiar with the Region's geography and demographics may not be surprised by the findings, but newcomers to the Region or those who haven't explored it much will see some interesting contrasts between the Region's rock 'n' roll heart and its country soul.

## An urban core with rural fringes

```{r}
#| label: district-inline-objects
#| include: false

# Population, land area and density, with the seven municipalities collapsed
# into Cities and Townships and into Region overall.
#
# Population and land area are sums. Density is not: averaging seven densities
# would give Wellesley the same weight as Kitchener and come out far too low.
# It has to be the group's people divided by the group's land, which is why it
# is worked out after the summarise() rather than carried through it.
grouped_land_pop_figures <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    city_pop         = sum(population[district_type == "City"]),
    city_area        = sum(area_sq_km[district_type == "City"]),
    township_pop     = sum(population[district_type == "Township"]),
    township_area    = sum(area_sq_km[district_type == "Township"]),
    region_pop       = sum(population),
    region_area      = sum(area_sq_km),
    city_density     = city_pop / city_area,
    township_density = township_pop / township_area,
    region_density   = region_pop / region_area,
    density_ratio    = city_density / township_density,
    city_pop_share   = city_pop / region_pop,
    township_pop_share = township_pop / region_pop,
    township_area_share = township_area / region_area
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(ends_with("share"), \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 1)),  # 15%
    across(ends_with("ratio"), \(x) comma(x, accuracy = 0.1)),  # 2.7
    across(where(is.numeric), \(x) comma(x, accuracy = 1))        # 631,721
  )

# Turn each column into its own object (city_pop, region_density, etc.)
list2env(grouped_land_pop_figures, environment()) |> invisible()

```

If you haven't spent much time driving through the townships, you may have no idea how vast they are relative to the cities. On a map, it looks like they're chomping the urban core they nearly surround. Collectively, the townships cover `r township_area` square km, or `r township_area_share` of the Region's `r region_area` square km. Even the smallest township, North Dumfries, is considerably larger than Kitchener, the biggest city. Judged solely by its area then, the Region is largely rural in character.

```{r}
#| label: land-mass
#| output: asis

# The seven municipal polygons, moved into EPSG:3161 - a projection made for
# Ontario, on which shapes this size keep their true proportions. The data is
# stored in plain latitude and longitude, which is convenient but draws a map
# slightly stretched, so the projection is chosen here rather than in the data.
districts_3161 <- st_transform(districts, 3161)

# Three labels need moving off the anchor stored in the data. It is the point
# furthest from any border, which is the roomiest spot but not always the one
# that looks centred once the words are drawn: Waterloo's sat half over its
# western border, Cambridge's ran past its eastern one, and once each name
# gained a line of land area underneath it and moved up to make room, North
# Dumfries' ran into the tongue of Cambridge that reaches into it. Metres east
# and north in EPSG:3161, arrived at by rendering the map and looking at it -
# the phone version especially, where the words are larger against the shapes.
# Waterloo's was measured rather than judged: its name is shifted until the
# nearest border point on its left is as far away as the nearest on its right,
# which on its slanting north-west edge is further east than it looks.
nudge <- tribble(
  ~district,         ~dx,    ~dy,
  "Waterloo",        2000,   1200,
  "Cambridge",        350,  -2200,
  "North Dumfries", -1000,   -300
)

# Label positions. 02_clean_data.R worked out where each label should sit and
# stored it as a longitude and latitude; here that becomes a point, moves into
# the map's projection, and is turned back into plain x and y columns so the
# nudges above can simply be added to it.
#
# "Township" goes on a second line rather than after the name, so that even
# "N. Dumfries Township" stays narrow enough to sit inside its own boundary.
# cwr_short_name() gives the house short form of a long municipal name; the
# nudges above are still keyed by the full name.
labels <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("label_lon", "label_lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3161) |>
  (\(points) bind_cols(
    st_drop_geometry(points),
    st_coordinates(points) |> as_tibble() |> set_names(c("x", "y"))
  ))() |>
  left_join(nudge, join_by(district)) |>
  mutate(
    # Every district that needs no nudge has no row in the table above
    x = x + replace_na(dx, 0),
    y = y + replace_na(dy, 0),
    label = if_else(
      district_type == "Township",
      paste0(cwr_short_name(district), "\nTownship"),
      cwr_short_name(district)
    ),
    # Land area, on its own line under the name. Whole square kilometres: the
    # boundary file gives four decimal places, which no one reading a map needs.
    area_label = paste0(label_comma(accuracy = 1)(area_sq_km), " km\u00b2"),
    # White on the dark city blue, black on the light township blue, where
    # white would be too faint to read
    text_colour = if_else(district_type == "City", "white", "black")
  )

p <- ggplot() +
  # Filled in the same two colours the bar chart uses, so a reader who has seen
  # one chart already knows which shapes are cities and which are townships.
  # The borders are white rather than a darker line: against filled shapes they
  # separate neighbours without drawing a second thing to look at, and around
  # the outside they disappear into the page, which leaves the Region as a
  # silhouette rather than a boxed-in diagram.
  geom_sf(
    data = districts_3161, aes(fill = district_type),
    colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  # The name sits just above the label point and the area just below it, so the
  # pair is centred where the name alone used to be. vjust = 0 puts a label's
  # bottom edge on its point and vjust = 1 puts its top edge there; the nudges
  # open a small gap between the two, in metres, because that is the unit of
  # the map's projection.
  geom_text(
    data = labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, colour = text_colour),
    size = label_size, lineheight = 1.05, fontface = "bold",
    vjust = 0, nudge_y = 250
  ) +
  # Plain rather than bold, and a little smaller, so the name still reads first
  # and the figure reads as a note on it. No box behind it: the text colour is
  # already chosen to read on its fill, and a box would cover the shape.
  geom_text(
    data = labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = area_label, colour = text_colour),
    size = label_size * 0.85,
    vjust = 1, nudge_y = -250
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = dodgerblue50),
    guide = "none"   # the labels on the shapes say which is which
  ) +
  # text_colour holds literal colour names: use them as they are
  scale_colour_identity() +
  # datum = NA drops the graticule - the faint grid of latitude and longitude
  # lines coord_sf() draws by default - which this map has no use for.
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "The townships appear to swallow their urban core",
    subtitle = "Cities and townships, land mass",
    caption = cwr_caption("Statistics Canada, 2021 census boundary files")
  ) +
  # theme_cwr() is built for charts with axes; a map wants none of them. Each
  # element is named individually because the theme sets them individually, and
  # a blanket axis.text would not override the more specific setting.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(), axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-districts",
  alt = paste0(
    "Outline map of Waterloo Region showing the borders of its seven ",
    "municipalities, each labelled with its name and land area: the cities of ",
    "Kitchener, Waterloo and Cambridge grouped together in the middle, ringed ",
    "by Woolwich Township to the north, Wellesley Township to the north west, ",
    "Wilmot Township to the south west and North Dumfries Township to the ",
    "south. Land areas in square kilometres: ",
    # Built from the labelled rows, like every other figure in an alt text here
    paste(
      paste(labels$district, label_comma(accuracy = 1)(labels$area_sq_km)),
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    "."
  ),
  # The phone map is half as wide but its text is drawn at the same size, so the
  # three cities in the middle cannot hold their labels without a further
  # reduction. 0.55 is where they sit clear of each other and of the borders
  # now that each carries a second line; it was 0.60 with names alone.
  height = 7.6, phone_height = 5.0, phone_text_scale = 0.55
)
```

## More cows than people?!

The latest StatsCan population estimates show that Kitchener has by far the most residents in the Region, with slightly more even than the other two cities combined. Together, the cities had a population of `r city_pop` , making up `r city_pop_share` of the Region's `r region_pop` residents in 2025. So despite covering `r township_area_share` of the Region's land, the townships contain only a sliver of its residents. Having a combined density of only `r township_density` residents per square km, the townships contain one resident for every `r density_ratio` city residents. With all that land and so few people, there's lots of room for cows!

```{r}
#| label: sizes
#| output: asis

# How far the axis runs, in residents, on each version of the chart. The density
# boxes hang from the right-hand edge of the panel, so this is also what sets
# the gap between the end of Kitchener's bar (about 324,000) and its box.
#
# The two versions need different numbers. A box is a fixed width in points,
# and the phone's panel is less than half as wide, so in residents a box is more
# than twice as wide there: a range that leaves a neat gap on a desktop puts the
# phone's box on top of the bar. So each gets its own, both read off a render,
# and the phone's is swapped in through cwr_figure() below.
axis_max <- 375000
axis_max_phone <- 470000

# Roughly how many characters of label fit across the whole phone axis, from
# zero to `axis_max_phone`. Used only to decide which labels go inside their
# bars; the phone is the narrower render, so a label that fits there fits on a
# desktop too.
axis_chars <- 30

population_bars <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    # fct_reorder() sorts ascending and a horizontal bar chart draws the first
    # level at the bottom, so the largest municipality ends up on top.
    district = fct_reorder(district, population),
    label = label_comma(accuracy = 1)(population),
    density_label = label_comma(accuracy = 1)(density_per_sq_km),
    # Whether a population label fits inside its bar. What decides it is the
    # width of the text in the axis's own units: one character is
    # axis_max_phone / axis_chars residents wide, and a label needs its length plus
    # a space or so of padding. The townships' bars are far too short; the
    # cities' are not.
    inside = population >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (axis_max_phone / axis_chars)
  )

p <- ggplot(population_bars, aes(x = population, y = district, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline the bars grow from. theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
  # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
  #
  # A segment rather than geom_vline(), which would run the full height of the
  # panel - up through the space left for the column heading. On a discrete
  # scale the rows sit at 1, 2, 3 ... and each bar is 0.7 tall, so running from
  # 0.5 to half a row past the top one stops the line just beyond the bars at
  # both ends.
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0.5, yend = nrow(population_bars) + 0.5,
    colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Inside the bar end, or just past it - hjust flips the text about its
      # anchor, and the anchor is the end of the bar either way
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      # White inside the dark city bars only; inside the light township
      # bars, and outside any bar, black reads better
      colour = if_else(inside & district_type == "City", "white", "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # Density, boxed in a column of its own rather than drawn as a second set of
  # bars. It is a different unit from the bars beside it, and a column of
  # numbers reads as a second fact about each row without competing for the eye.
  # x = Inf is the right-hand edge of the panel, whatever the axis range, and
  # hjust = 1 hangs each box from it. That is what lets the phone's wider range
  # move the column without a second set of layers.
  geom_label(
    aes(x = Inf, label = density_label),
    hjust = 1,
    size = label_size * 0.8,
    fill = "grey90",
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0,
    label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines")
  ) +
  # The column's heading, in the room the y scale below leaves above the top
  # row. y = Inf is the top edge of the panel and vjust = 1 hangs the box from
  # it. (The industry chart this pattern came from lifted its heading above the
  # panel instead, but that chart had an axis row up there to make space; this
  # one has none, so a lifted heading ran into the subtitle.) hjust = 1
  # right-aligns the two lines with each other and with the figures under them.
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = Inf, y = Inf, label = "Residents\nper km\u00b2",
    hjust = 1, vjust = 1, lineheight = 1.0,
    size = label_size * 0.8,
    fontface = "plain",
    fill = "grey90", colour = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0,
    label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines")
  ) +
  # The colours above are literal colour names rather than groups to map, which
  # is what scale_colour_identity() means: use the value, do not look it up
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = dodgerblue50),
    guide = "none"   # the colours are explained by the bars themselves
  ) +
  # The axis runs out to the box column and no further
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, axis_max), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  # An extra row and a half of space above Kitchener, which is where the column
  # heading hangs. add is in rows, because the scale is discrete.
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1.6)), labels = cwr_short_name) +
  # Stops the heading and any label that overhangs the panel from being cut off
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "The townships are very sparsely populated compared to the cities",
    subtitle = "Cities and townships, population, 2025",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      c("Statistics Canada Table 17-10-0155-01",
        "the 2021 census boundary files"),
      credit = TRUE
    )
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

# The figures in the alt text are built from the same rows the bars are drawn
# from, not typed out. Typed, they would be right today and quietly wrong the
# first time an estimate is revised - and wrong only for the readers who cannot
# see the chart to check it against.
alt_entries <- population_bars |>
  arrange(desc(population)) |>
  mutate(entry = paste0(district, " ", label, " residents, ",
                        density_label, " per square kilometre")) |>
  pull(entry)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-sizes",
  alt = paste0(
    "Horizontal bars of population, one per municipality, largest first, with ",
    "the three cities in dark blue and the four townships in light blue, and each ",
    "municipality's residents per square kilometre boxed in a column on the ",
    "right. ",
    paste(alt_entries, collapse = "; "), "."
  ),
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
  # The phone's longer axis, for the reason given at the top of the chunk.
  # Adding a scale of a type already present replaces it.
  phone = list(
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, axis_max_phone), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0)))
  )
)
```

When I first drafted the preceding analysis, my cow references were made in jest, as indicated by the heading's [interrobang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interrobang).

```{r}
#| label: cattle
#| output: asis

# The four townships added together: all cattle and every resident, counted on
# the same day - 11 May 2021, census day for both the Census of Agriculture and
# the Census of Population. sum() is used without na.rm = TRUE on purpose: if
# the quality check in 02_clean_data.R had blanked a township's figure, the
# total would come out missing rather than quietly short.
cattle_people <- cattle |>
  summarise(Cattle = sum(cattle), People = sum(population)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "what", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    # A horizontal chart draws the first level at the bottom, so the order is
    # reversed to put cattle on top
    what = fct_rev(fct_inorder(what)),
    label = label_comma(accuracy = 1)(count),
    # Whether a label fits inside its bar, the same test as the other bar
    # charts: the axis runs to about 1.2 times the longest bar, and roughly 45
    # characters of label fit across it on a phone.
    inside = count >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(count) * 1.2 / 45)
  )

p <- ggplot(cattle_people, aes(x = count, y = what, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline, as a segment that stops just past the two bars rather than a
  # line the full height of the panel (see the population chart above)
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0.5, yend = nrow(cattle_people) + 0.5,
    colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Inside the bar end, or just past it
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      # White on the dark blue only; on the silver, and outside a bar, black
      # reads better
      colour = if_else(inside & what == "Cattle", "white", "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(Cattle = dodgerblue, People = cowboysilver),
    guide = "none"   # each bar is named on the axis
  ) +
  # Room on the right for a label that sits outside its bar
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Cattle and people in the four townships, 2021",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      c("Statistics Canada Tables 32-10-0370-01", "98-10-0002-01"),
      credit = TRUE
    )
  ) +
  # Both bars carry their number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

# Built from the plotted figures, like every alt text in the post
alt_figures <- cattle_people |>
  arrange(desc(what)) |>
  mutate(entry = paste0(str_to_lower(what), " ", label)) |>
  pull(entry)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-cattle",
  alt = paste0(
    "Two horizontal bars for North Dumfries, Wellesley, Wilmot and Woolwich ",
    "townships together on 11 May 2021: cattle in blue and people in grey. ",
    str_to_sentence(paste(alt_figures, collapse = "; ")), "."
  )
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

## Income



```{r}
#| label: income
#| output: asis

# The two measures: the column each comes from and the heading its panel
# carries. Kept in a table for the same reason as the chart above - the panel
# headings and the alt text are then built from one list and cannot drift
# apart. There is no separate spoken form here because both headings read
# aloud exactly as they are written.
income_measures <- tribble(
  ~column,                   ~panel,
  "household_income_2026",   "Household",
  "individual_income_2026",  "Individual"
)

income_panels <- income |>
  select(district, district_type, household_income_2026, individual_income_2026) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(household_income_2026, individual_income_2026),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(income_measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(panel, levels = income_measures$panel),
    # Each panel is ordered by its own figures rather than sharing one order,
    # so a place can sit seventh for household income and third for individual
    # income. That disagreement between the two panels is the point of putting
    # them side by side.
    #
    # ggplot2 has one discrete scale for the whole chart, so a factor of place
    # names can carry only one order. The way round it is to make each bar's
    # identity the place *and* its panel - "Kitchener|Median individual income"
    # - and sort that combined key by value. Drawn with a free y scale, each
    # panel shows only its own eight levels in its own order, and the scale
    # below strips the panel name off again before the label is drawn.
    # (tidytext::reorder_within() does exactly this. It is two lines here, so
    # the package is not worth adding.)
    #
    # fct_reorder() sorts ascending and a horizontal bar chart draws the first
    # level at the bottom, so the highest income ends up on top of its panel.
    row = fct_reorder(paste(district, measure, sep = "|"), value),
    # Rounded to the nearest hundred dollars. The census medians themselves are
    # rounded before publication, and multiplying by an index does not add
    # precision, so a figure to the dollar would be false exactness.
    label = label_currency(accuracy = 100, big.mark = ",")(value)
  )

p <- ggplot(income_panels, aes(x = value, y = row, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline the bars grow from; theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
  # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Every label sits inside its bar end. The shortest bar here still holds
      # its label comfortably, so unlike the chart above there is no test for
      # which ones have to move outside.
      #
      # White on the dark city blue only. On the light township blue and the
      # Region's silver, white is a contrast ratio of under three to one, which
      # is too faint to read at this size, so those labels are black.
      colour = if_else(district_type == "City", "white", "black")
    ),
    hjust = 1.15,
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # The colours above are literal colour names rather than groups to map, which
  # is what scale_colour_identity() means: use the value, do not look it up
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = dodgerblue50, Region = cowboysilver),
    guide = "none"   # the colours are explained by the bars themselves
  ) +
  # A little air at the bar ends so the longest bar does not touch the panel
  # edge. No room is needed on the right for outside labels, as there are none.
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  # Everything from the "|" on is the panel name carried by the sort key above,
  # and is not for reading. What is left is the name, in its house short form.
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) cwr_short_name(str_split_i(x, fixed("|"), 1))) +
  # Free on y, fixed on x. Free on y is what lets each panel hold its own
  # order, and it is why the second panel carries its own row labels: the rows
  # are no longer the same rows in the same places.
  #
  # x stays shared, which is the other point of the chart: a household is more
  # than one earner, and at one scale the individual bars come out visibly
  # shorter. Given its own scale - as the charts above do, where the measures
  # are people, square kilometres and a density - the second panel would look
  # like the first and that comparison would be lost.
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Households and individuals in the townships outearn those in the cities",
    subtitle = "Median total income in 2020<sup>1</sup> of people living in private dwellings, 2026 dollars<sup>2</sup>",
    # One footnote, keyed to whatever in the title or subtitle needs it.
    caption = cwr_caption(
      c("Statistics Canada Tables 98-10-0057-01, 98-10-0070-01", "and 18-10-0004-01"),
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c("latest year available, from 2021 census", "adjusted by the Ontario all-items CPI")
      # No sampling note: census medians are published for 100% of the
      # population, from tax records linked to every respondent
    )
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed, for the reason given above.
alt_lines <- income_panels |>
  # Each line reads down its own panel, highest first, as the bars are drawn
  arrange(measure, desc(value)) |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = measure
  ) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(measure, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-income",
  alt = paste0(
    "Two panels of horizontal bars, one row per municipality and one for ",
    "Waterloo Region as a whole, with the three cities in dark blue, the four ",
    "townships in light blue and the Region in grey. Each panel is ordered by its own ",
    "figures, highest at the top, and both are drawn to the same dollar scale. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
  # Two panels side by side will not fit across a phone, so the phone version
  # stacks them. Adding a facet replaces the one above.
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y"))
)
```

## Households

```{r}
#| label: households
#| output: asis

# Two measures, each with its own unit, so each panel gets its own scale and its
# own number format. The panel heading carries the unit wherever the label
# cannot: "3.4" says nothing on its own, "85%" says most of it.
# Roughly how many characters of label fit across one panel of a two-panel
# chart at this font size, the way `panel_chars` above does for three panels.
# Also used by the mother tongue charts below.
panel_chars_wide <- 45

household_measures <- tribble(
  ~column,                    ~panel,                                   ~accuracy, ~suffix,
  "average_household_size",   "Average private household size, number of persons",            0.1,      "",
  "single_detached_percent",  "Single-detached houses, as % of private dwellings",  1,        "%"
)

household_panels <- households |>
  # One order for both panels, set on the first, so a place sits on the same row
  # in each and can be read straight across.
  mutate(district = fct_reorder(district, average_household_size)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(average_household_size, single_detached_percent),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(household_measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(panel, levels = household_measures$panel),
    label = label_number(accuracy = accuracy, suffix = suffix)(value)
  ) |>
  # Whether a label fits inside its bar, asked panel by panel because each panel
  # has its own scale. Same test as the population chart above, but a panel here
  # is wider - two panels to the page rather than three - so more characters fit
  # across it. Read off a render, as the other number was.
  mutate(
    inside = value >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars_wide),
    .by = measure
  )

p <- ggplot(household_panels, aes(x = value, y = district, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline the bars grow from; theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
  # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Inside the bar end, or just past it - hjust flips the text about its
      # anchor, and the anchor is the end of the bar either way
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      # White inside the dark city bars only; inside the light township
      # bars, and outside any bar, black reads better
      colour = if_else(inside & district_type == "City", "white", "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # The colours above are literal colour names rather than groups to map, which
  # is what scale_colour_identity() means: use the value, do not look it up
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = dodgerblue50),
    guide = "none"   # the same two colours as every other chart in the post
  ) +
  # Room on the right for any label that sits outside its bar
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  # The house short form of a long municipal name
  scale_y_discrete(labels = cwr_short_name) +
  # Free on x only, because the two measures share no unit. The rows are shared,
  # so only the first panel carries the place names.
  # label_wrap_gen() breaks a heading too wide for its panel onto a second line;
  # panel headings are drawn by the theme as plain text, so cwr_wrap() - which
  # emits <br> - would show its markup instead of acting on it.
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), nrow = 1, scales = "free_x",
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(26)) +
  # Stops a label that overhangs the panel edge from being cut off
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption("Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0041-01", credit = TRUE)
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed, as above. Each line reads down
# its panel in the order the rows are drawn, top first.
alt_lines <- household_panels |>
  arrange(measure, desc(district)) |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = measure
  ) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(measure, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-households",
  alt = paste0(
    "Two panels of horizontal bars, one row per municipality, both ordered by ",
    "average household size, with the three cities in dark blue and the four ",
    "townships in light blue. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
  # Two panels side by side will not fit across a phone, so the phone version
  # stacks them. Adding a facet replaces the one above.
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free_x",
                          labeller = label_wrap_gen(26)))
)
```

## Language

::: panel-tabset
### Mother tongue is not English or French

```{r}
#| label: language-other
#| output: asis

# The two measures, one to a tab. The second is a share of a share - German or
# Pennsylvania German among those whose mother tongue is neither English nor
# French. Both are percentages, but of different denominators, so each chart
# keeps its own scale.
language_bars_data <- language |>
  # One order for both tabs, set on the first, so a place stays on the same row
  # when the reader switches tabs and only its bar changes length.
  mutate(district = fct_reorder(district, non_official_percent)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(non_official_percent, german_percent_of_non_official),
    names_to = "measure", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = label_number(accuracy = 1, suffix = "%")(value)) |>
  # Whether a label fits inside its bar, the same test as the population chart,
  # asked for each measure on its own because each chart has its own scale. The
  # axis runs to about 1.2 times the longest bar. A single panel across a phone
  # is about as wide as one panel of a two-panel desktop chart, so
  # `panel_chars_wide` from the household chart holds here too.
  mutate(
    inside = value >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars_wide),
    .by = measure
  )

# Both tabs draw the same chart from a different measure, so it is built once
# here. Titles, subtitles and captions differ, so each tab adds its own labs().
language_bars <- function(which) {
  bars <- language_bars_data |> filter(measure == which)

  ggplot(bars, aes(x = value, y = district, fill = district_type)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.7) +
    # The baseline the bars grow from; theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
    # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = label,
        # Inside the bar end, or just past it
        hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
        # White inside the dark city bars only; inside the light township
        # bars, and outside any bar, black reads better
        colour = if_else(inside & district_type == "City", "white", "black")
      ),
      size = label_size * 0.8
    ) +
    scale_colour_identity() +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = dodgerblue50),
      guide = "none"
    ) +
    # Room on the right for any label that sits outside its bar
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
    # The house short form of a long municipal name
    scale_y_discrete(labels = cwr_short_name) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
      axis.line.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
    )
}

# Alt text read top to bottom, in the order the rows are drawn
language_alt <- function(which) {
  language_bars_data |>
    filter(measure == which) |>
    arrange(desc(district)) |>
    summarise(entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", ")) |>
    pull(entries)
}

# Said once, in both tabs' captions
mother_tongue_note <- "Mother tongue is the language first learned at home in childhood and still understood"

p <- language_bars("non_official_percent") +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0180-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = mother_tongue_note
    )
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-language-other",
  alt = paste0(
    "Horizontal bars, one row per municipality, showing the percentage of ",
    "people whose mother tongue is neither English nor French, highest at the ",
    "top, with the three cities in dark blue and the four townships in light blue. ",
    language_alt("non_official_percent"), "."
  )
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```

### Is German or Pennsylvania German

```{r}
#| label: language-german

p <- language_bars("german_percent_of_non_official") +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0180-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(mother_tongue_note, "German and Pennsylvania German counted together")
    )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-language-german",
  alt = paste0(
    "Horizontal bars, one row per municipality, showing the percentage of ",
    "people with a mother tongue other than English or French whose mother ",
    "tongue is German or Pennsylvania German. Rows are in the same order as the ",
    "previous tab, not by these figures. The three cities are in dark blue and the ",
    "four townships in light blue. ",
    language_alt("german_percent_of_non_official"), "."
  )
  # No height given: cwr_figure() sets it from the number of rows.
)
```
